title: "Not a believer": Congressman, whose district is potential Bigfoot stomping ground, dismisses sighting reports by Trump's disclosure
excerpt: Representative Cliff Bentz, the Oregon Republican whose district takes in forest land named in the federal government's newly released Bigfoot files, is not convinced by the renewed Sasquatch talk. Bentz told TMZ he is "not a believer in Bigfoot.
content:
Vatsala Chauhan

Updated Thu, November 26, 2026 at 12:26 PM UTC

Representative Cliff Bentz, the Oregon Republican whose district takes in forest land named in the federal government's newly released Bigfoot files, is not convinced by the renewed Sasquatch talk. Bentz told TMZ he is "not a believer in Bigfoot."

His evidence is personal. Bentz said he grew up on a cattle ranch and rode horseback through Oregon's Malheur National Forest for hundreds of hours between the ages of 14 and 22, according to TMZ. In that time, he said, he never saw a single track or anything else that suggested the creature was alive. He told the outlet he never ran into anyone in a scruffy Bigfoot costume either.

More on the story below.

Asked about the purported Sasquatch photographs that have circulated for decades, Bentz recommended focusing "more on tracks" as possible evidence, TMZ reported. He still regards the whole business as nonsense.

The three documents, filed under the title "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records," were posted to the U.S. Forest Service's public reading room on October 15 without a formal announcement, as The Washington Post reported. TMZ, the New York Post and Newsweek picked them up in the past week and treated the release as a Trump administration disclosure; the Forest Service is part of the Department of Agriculture.

What the 1982 file actually concluded

The centerpiece is a six-page memo from 1982 by Rodney L. Johnson, a wildlife biologist assigned by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to examine large footprints at three sites in the Umatilla National Forest, which runs across northeast Oregon and southeast Washington.

Bentz represents the Oregon portion. Johnson concluded that tracks at two of the sites were made by "something other than a 300-pound plus two-footed being," while allowing that "if the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail."

A second memo, from Border Patrol tracker Joel Hardin, went further, describing the prints as "a very clever attempt to perpetrate a hoax" and suggesting they had been made with a fake foot of rubber or soft plaster, The Telegraph reported. The remaining files, a 1980 letter about tracks a hunting party found near Petty Creek, Montana, and a 2003 newspaper article about hundreds of prints in snow near a sawmill, record what witnesses reported without settling anything.

Nothing in the release shows that Sasquatch exists, and the government's own biologist reached much the same verdict on the footprints as Bentz. He won a fourth term on November 3 with about 61.6% of the vote, according to results compiled by OPB and Jefferson Public Radio.
